registry_T4_chapter_digests.chapter_rolling_summary: Lockwood narrates his first visit to Wuthering Heights in 1801. He meets his landlord, Mr. Heathcliff, whose reserved and suspicious manner fascinates him. After entering the bleak, old house and noting its strange architecture, furnishings, and the name Hareton Earnshaw carved above the door, Lockwood reflects at length on Heathcliff’s character and on his own awkwardness in human relations. Left briefly alone, he attempts to pet a dog and provokes a violent attack from several of the house dogs, until a kitchen woman intervenes. Heathcliff responds with brusque indifference, then offers wine and becomes somewhat more civil. Despite clear signs that Heathcliff does not welcome company, Lockwood decides he will visit again.

scene_summaries.summary: Lockwood recounts his first call on Mr. Heathcliff at Wuthering Heights, observes the house and its inhabitants, suffers a dog attack, then shares strained but slightly thawing conversation and resolves to return.

candidate_transition.note: after Lockwood's sharp reply, Heathcliff grins and the exchange becomes briefly more convivial

unresolved_threads.description: Why Heathcliff lives as a gentleman in such a rough household, and what his background is, remains unclear.
The significance of the carved name 'Hareton Earnshaw' over the door is not explained.
Lockwood plans another visit although Heathcliff seems not to want one.

translator_relevant_facts.fact: The chapter is first-person narration by Lockwood, recounting his immediate experience with ironic self-commentary.
Heathcliff's dialogue is clipped, terse, and brusque, often marked by compressed phrasing.
Joseph speaks in a marked religious, peevish manner that should sound rustic and old-fashioned.
'Wuthering' is explicitly glossed as a provincial adjective describing turbulent weather exposure.
The main room called 'the house' functions as combined sitting-room/kitchen/parlour in local usage.
Lockwood is Heathcliff's new tenant at Thrushcross Grange, which shapes their guarded politeness.
Lockwood's narration mixes formal politeness in speech with sardonic, elaborate descriptive prose.
